subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Think about the water your family drinks. If it comes from a well, a river like the Jubba, or a rain barrel, it is almost never truly clean. It carries bits of sand, mud, tiny living germs, and sometimes dissolved salt you cannot even see. Now think about the salt your mother sprinkles into a pot of bariis, or the sugar that sweetens a glass of shaah. Both of these were once locked inside something else — salt inside sea water, sugar inside a sugar-cane plant — and clever people used science to pull them out. In this unit you will learn the science of mixtures and how to separate them. It is one of the most practical, life-saving topics in all of chemistry.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Know that purity is a way to describe how much of a specific chemical is in a mixture.
Understand that the concentration of a solution relates to how many particles of the solute are present in a volume of the solvent.
Describe how paper chromatography can be used to separate and identify substances in a sample.
Describe how the solubility of different salts varies with temperature.

objectives.subStrand: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions
objectives.text: Present and interpret observations and measurements appropriately.

outcomes: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
Explain the difference between a pure substance and a mixture, and give everyday examples of each.
Define and use the words solution, solvent, solute and dissolve correctly.
Describe what solubility means and list the factors that make a solid dissolve faster.
Explain what a saturated solution is and how it forms.
Choose and describe the correct separation method — filtration, evaporation, crystallisation, distillation or chromatography — for a given mixture.
Explain how each separation method works using the different properties of the substances involved.
Apply these methods to real problems such as getting clean water from muddy or salty water.
Read and interpret a simple solubility result and a chromatography result.
Study this table carefully. These words are the tools of a chemist who works with mixtures. Notice how the example column ties each word to something you already know from home.

concepts.title: Pure Substances and Mixtures
concepts.explanation:
The first big idea in this unit is the difference between something that is pure and something that is a mixture. In everyday speech, 'pure' can mean clean or natural. In science it has a much more exact meaning.

A pure substance is made of only one type of particle, with nothing else mixed in. Pure water contains only water particles. Pure salt contains only salt particles. Pure sugar contains only sugar particles. Because a pure substance is always the same all the way through, it behaves in a fixed, predictable way. For example, pure water always boils at exactly 100 degrees Celsius and always freezes at exactly 0 degrees Celsius at sea level. This fixed behaviour is actually a test for purity — if a scientist wants to check whether a sample of water is pure, one thing they can do is measure its boiling point.

A mixture is made of two or more substances that are simply mixed together and not chemically joined. This is the key point: in a mixture, each substance keeps its own properties and can be separated out again. When you stir salt into water, the salt does not turn into a new substance — it is still salt, just spread out among the water. If you remove the water, the salt comes back exactly as it was. This is why almost every method in this whole unit works: because the parts of a mixture keep their own properties, we can use the differences between those properties to pull the mixture apart.

Mixtures do not have a fixed boiling or melting point. Salty water, for example, boils at a slightly higher temperature than pure water, and the exact temperature depends on how much salt is dissolved in it. So a substance that boils over a range of temperatures, rather than at one exact temperature, is probably a mixture.

Look around and you will see that mixtures are everywhere, and pure substances are actually quite rare in nature. The air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other gases. Sea water is a mixture of water and many dissolved salts. Soil is a mixture of sand, clay, small stones and decayed plants. Camel milk is a mixture of water, fats, sugars and proteins. Even the smoke rising from a charcoal fire is a mixture of gases and tiny solid specks.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The salt we buy in shops is often not perfectly pure — it may have tiny amounts of other minerals mixed in, which is why some salt is slightly grey or pink. Rainwater is one of the purest natural waters, because it forms when water evaporates into the sky and leaves its dissolved salts and dirt behind — a natural distillation carried out by the sun.

concepts.title: Solutions, Solvents and Solutes
concepts.explanation:
One of the most important kinds of mixture is a solution. You make solutions every single day, probably without thinking about it. When your family makes shaah and stirs in sugar, the sugar seems to vanish. It has not disappeared — it has dissolved, and you have made a solution. Let us learn the proper words for what is going on.

Whenever something dissolves, three words describe what is happening:

The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving. In a glass of sweet shaah, the water is the solvent.

The solute is the substance that dissolves into the solvent. In sweet shaah, the sugar is the solute.

The solution is the clear mixture you get at the end — the solvent with the solute spread evenly through it.

A simple sentence links them all together: solute + solvent = solution. So sugar (the solute) plus water (the solvent) makes sugary water (the solution). Salt (the solute) plus water (the solvent) makes salty water (the solution). Water is by far the most common solvent in the world — it dissolves so many things that scientists sometimes call it the 'universal solvent'.

When a solid dissolves, its tiny particles break away from each other and spread out to fill the gaps between the particles of the liquid. Picture a spoonful of salt dropped into water. At first you can see the white grains. As they dissolve, the salt particles separate one by one and slip in among the water particles, spreading out until they are shared evenly through the whole glass. That is why a solution looks clear — the particles are far too small to see — and why the salt is now in every part of the water, not just at the bottom. Very importantly, the salt is not destroyed. Its particles are still there, hidden among the water. This is exactly why we can get the salt back later by evaporating the water.
concepts.example: Not everything dissolves. A substance that can dissolve in a particular liquid is called soluble; a substance that cannot is called insoluble. Salt and sugar are soluble in water. Sand, charcoal, chalk and cooking oil are insoluble in water — stir sand into water and, however long you wait, it just sinks to the bottom. This difference is enormously useful. If a solid is insoluble, we can catch it with a filter; if it is soluble, we cannot filter it out, and we must use evaporation or distillation instead. Knowing whether something is soluble is the first question a scientist asks when planning how to separate a mixture.

concepts.title: Solubility and Saturation
concepts.explanation:
Now we go a step deeper. It is not enough to know whether something dissolves — a good scientist also asks how much dissolves, and how fast. This is the idea of solubility.

Solubility tells us how much of a solute will dissolve in a certain amount of solvent at a given temperature. Some solutes are very soluble — you can dissolve a great deal of sugar in a cup of water. Others are only slightly soluble. Solubility is not a fixed, single number, because it depends strongly on the temperature of the solvent, as you will now see.

If you have ever waited for sugar to dissolve in cold water, you know it can be slow. Three things speed up dissolving, and you can feel each of them in your own kitchen:

Heating the solvent. Sugar and salt dissolve much faster in hot shaah than in cold water. Warmer particles move faster and pull the solute apart more quickly. Hot water also holds *more* solute in total.

Stirring. Stirring keeps fresh solvent moving past the solid, carrying dissolved particles away so more can dissolve. This is why you stir sugar into your tea.

Crushing the solid into smaller pieces. A powder dissolves faster than a big lump because more of its surface is touching the water. A block of rock salt dissolves slowly; ground salt dissolves quickly.

Notice that stirring and crushing make the solute dissolve faster, but they do not let you dissolve more in total. Only heating does both — it speeds things up and increases how much can dissolve.

Did You Know? Hot water can hold far more dissolved sugar than cold water. This is the secret behind making sweets and toffee: sugar is dissolved in very hot water and then, as it cools, the water can no longer hold it all and the sugar sets solid. Gases behave the opposite way to solids: a cold fizzy drink holds its gas better than a warm one, which is why a warm soda goes flat and foams over quickly.

There is a limit to how much you can dissolve. Keep adding salt to a glass of water and stirring, and at first it all disappears. But eventually you reach a point where no more salt will dissolve — the extra salt just sinks to the bottom and stays there, no matter how long you stir. When a solution is holding as much dissolved solute as it possibly can, we say it is a saturated solution.
concepts.example: Here is the interesting part. If you heat that saturated salt water, it can suddenly dissolve more salt, because solubility rises with temperature. And if you let a hot saturated solution cool down, it can no longer hold all the solute, so the extra solute comes out of the solution as solid crystals. This is a beautiful and useful idea, and it is exactly how the crystallisation method works, which you will meet in Part 4. A saturated solution sitting in the sun along the coast is how sea-salt farmers know their salt is about to appear.

concepts.title: Separation Methods
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to the heart of the unit: how to separate a mixture back into its parts. The golden rule is always the same — find a property that is different between the substances, and use that difference to separate them. A different particle size, whether something dissolves, a different boiling point, or how strongly a dye sticks to paper — each difference gives us a method. Let us take the five main methods in turn.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. You pour the mixture through a filter — filter paper in a laboratory, or a clean cloth or a fine sieve at home. The liquid passes through the tiny holes, but the solid bits are too big to fit through, so they are trapped. The two parts even have proper names: the solid trapped on the filter is called the residue, and the clear liquid that drips through is called the filtrate.

Filtration is one of the most useful skills in daily life. When your grandmother pours a pot of shaah through a strainer, the tea leaves (residue) stay behind and the clear tea (filtrate) flows into the cup. When a family in a village near Garissa pours muddy well water through a folded cloth, the mud and sand are caught and clearer water passes through. Remember one vital point, though: filtration removes only the solid bits you can catch. It does not remove dissolved salt, and it does not kill germs. Filtered water may look clear but can still make you very ill, so it must always be boiled before drinking to be truly safe.

Did You Know? A traditional cloth filter can remove the tiny water creatures that carry some diseases, which is why folding a clean cloth several times over a water pot has protected families for generations — but boiling is still needed to kill the smallest germs.

Evaporation does the opposite job to filtration — it separates a soluble solid from the liquid it is dissolved in. You cannot filter salt out of salty water, because the salt is dissolved and slips straight through the filter. Instead, you gently warm the solution so that the water turns into a gas (water vapour) and escapes into the air, leaving the solid behind. The solute stays because it does not evaporate at that temperature — only the water does.

This is exactly how sea salt is harvested along the Indian Ocean coast near Berbera and Kismaayo. Sea water is let into shallow pans, and the hot sun slowly evaporates the water. Day by day the water disappears into the air, and the salt is left behind in the pan, ready to be scooped up, dried and sold. It is powered by nothing but sunshine — a free and clever use of evaporation that has fed and preserved food for thousands of years.

Crystallisation is a gentler, more careful cousin of evaporation. It is used when you want to collect the solute as beautiful, well-formed crystals rather than a rough powder. You warm the solution to evaporate some — but not all — of the water, until the solution is saturated. Then you stop heating and let it cool slowly. As it cools, the solubility drops, the solution can no longer hold all its solute, and the solute comes out slowly as solid crystals. The slower it cools, the larger and neater the crystals grow.

You have almost certainly seen crystallisation without naming it. Rock sugar (sometimes called sugar crystals) is made this way, and so are the large flat crystals of sea salt. The difference between evaporation and crystallisation is subtle but real: evaporation drives off *all* the water quickly and leaves a dry solid, while crystallisation removes only *some* water and then cools the solution to grow clean, pure crystals. If a chemist wants a pure, well-shaped product, they choose crystallisation.

Sometimes it is not the solid you want — it is the pure liquid. If you have salty water and you want to drink the water, evaporation is no use, because it lets the precious water escape into the air and keeps only the salt. Distillation solves this problem cleverly by catching the escaping vapour and cooling it back into a liquid.

Here is how it works, step by step. You boil the salty water. The water turns to steam and rises, but the salt cannot turn to a gas at that temperature, so the salt stays behind in the container. The steam then travels to a cool surface, where it condenses — cools and turns back into liquid water. Because only the water evaporated and then condensed, the liquid you collect is pure water, with the salt left behind. In a laboratory the cooling is done in a tube called a condenser; at home, steam condenses on a cool pot lid and drips off.

Distillation is how ships at sea and desert towns turn salty sea water into fresh drinking water, and it is one of the most important technologies for regions that face drought. It also explains a natural wonder: the sun distils the ocean every single day. Water evaporates from the sea, rises, cools high in the sky, condenses into clouds, and falls as clean rain — leaving all the sea salt behind. Rain is nature's distilled water.

Did You Know? Distillation uses two changes of state you already know: boiling (liquid to gas) and condensing (gas back to liquid). No new substance is made — the water is just taken apart from the salt and put back together, pure. A large desalination plant on the coast can distil millions of litres of sea water into fresh water every day to supply a whole city.

The last method looks almost like magic. Chromatography separates different coloured dyes that are mixed together in a liquid, such as the many colours hidden inside a single ink or food dye. You put a small spot of the coloured mixture near the bottom of a strip of paper, then stand the paper so its bottom edge just touches a shallow pool of water (the solvent), without the spot itself touching the water.

The water slowly soaks up the paper, and as it rises it carries the dyes with it. Here is the clever part: different dyes are carried at different speeds. A dye that dissolves easily and does not stick to the paper is carried far and fast. A dye that sticks tightly to the paper and dissolves less easily is left behind, low down. So a single black spot may separate into several bands of colour spread up the paper — perhaps blue, red and yellow all hiding inside one 'black' ink. Each dye is separated because of a difference in how strongly it holds to the paper versus how well it dissolves in the moving solvent.
concepts.example: Chromatography is used by real scientists to check what colours are in food, to test whether a medicine is pure, and even by detectives to compare inks on a document. And you can do it at home with nothing but a paper towel, a felt-tip pen and a little water.

concepts.title: Choosing the Right Method
concepts.explanation:
A real scientist does not just know the methods — they know which one to choose for a given mixture. This is where all your learning comes together. To choose correctly, ask yourself a short chain of questions about the mixture:

Is it a solid mixed with a liquid? If the solid is insoluble (like sand or mud), use filtration. If the solid is dissolved (soluble), filtration will not work.

Do I want to keep the dissolved solid? If yes, use evaporation (for a quick dry solid) or crystallisation (for pure, well-formed crystals).

Do I want to keep the liquid itself, pure? Then use distillation, which catches and cools the vapour.

Am I separating coloured dyes in a liquid? Then use chromatography.
concepts.example: The key to every choice is the same golden rule: look for the property that is different. Is one part insoluble while the other dissolves? Filter. Does one part evaporate while the other stays? Evaporate or distil. Do the dyes move at different speeds? Use chromatography. Once you can name the difference, the method almost chooses itself.

concepts.title: A worked real-life example - cleaning muddy, salty water
concepts.explanation:
Imagine a family during a drought has only muddy water that is also slightly salty, and they want clean drinking water. No single method does it all — you must combine them in the right order:

Filter first. Pour the muddy water through a clean cloth to catch the mud and sand (the insoluble residue). Now the water is clear but still salty and may still hold germs.

Distil next, if salt must be removed. Boil the clear water and catch and cool the steam to collect pure water, leaving the dissolved salt behind.

If there is no salt to remove, simply boil the filtered water. Boiling kills the germs that filtration cannot remove. Filtered water that has been boiled is safe to drink.
concepts.example: Notice why the order matters. If you tried to distil the muddy water without filtering it first, the mud would make a burnt mess in the pot. Filtering first protects the later steps. Choosing the right method and the right order is the mark of a careful scientist.

methods.title: Cleaning Muddy Water by Filtration
methods.example: To use filtration to separate the mud and sand out of dirty water, and to see what filtration can and cannot do.
steps: Stir the soil into the water so you have a good muddy mixture. Look at it and note its colour.
Fold the cloth several times to make a thick filter, and lay it over the mouth of an empty clean cup.
Slowly pour the muddy water through the cloth into the cup. Do not let it overflow.
Look at the water that has passed through (the filtrate) and at the cloth (the residue).
If the water is still cloudy, pour it through a fresh part of the cloth a second time.

methods.title: Getting Salt Back from Salt Water (Evaporation)
methods.example: To use evaporation to separate dissolved salt from water, just as sea-salt farmers do along the coast.
steps: Dissolve two or three spoonfuls of salt in a small cup of warm water. Stir until the water looks clear and you cannot see the salt any more.
Talk about it: the salt is the solute, the water is the solvent, and the clear salty water is the solution.
Pour a thin layer of the salt solution onto the dark plate.
Put the plate in a warm, sunny place where it will not be disturbed.
Check it once or twice a day for two to four days as the water slowly disappears.

methods.title: Hidden Colours: Paper Chromatography
methods.example: To use paper chromatography to separate a single ink or dye into the different colours hidden inside it.
steps: Draw a thick dot of ink about 2 cm up from the bottom end of the paper strip. Press hard so the colour is strong.
Pour about 1 cm of water into the cup.
Hang the strip so its bottom edge just dips into the water, but the ink dot stays ABOVE the water line. Tape the top to a pencil laid across the cup.
Watch as the water slowly climbs up the paper and reaches the ink dot.
Leave it for 10 to 20 minutes as the water carries the colours up the paper.

methods.title: The Dissolving and Saturation Test
methods.example: To investigate how temperature, stirring and grain size affect dissolving, and to make a saturated solution.
steps: Part A — Temperature: Put one level spoonful of salt into each of the cold, warm and hot cups at the same time. Do NOT stir. Watch and time how long each takes to disappear.
Part B — Stirring: Add another spoonful to the cold cup and this time stir it. Does it dissolve faster than the one you did not stir?
Part C — Grain size (optional): Drop a sugar cube and the same amount of loose sugar into two cups of the same temperature. Which dissolves first?
Part D — Saturation: Take the hot-water cup. Keep adding salt one spoonful at a time, stirring after each, and counting the spoonfuls, until no more will dissolve and it collects at the bottom.
Record all your results in the table.

methods.title: Catching Pure Water (Simple Distillation)
methods.example: To collect pure water from salty water by boiling it gently and catching the steam on a cool lid — a simple, safe model of distillation.
steps: An adult pours the salty water into the pot to a shallow depth, and stands the empty clean cup in the middle so its rim is above the water.
Put the lid on the pot UPSIDE DOWN (so the dome points inwards, guiding drips towards the cup).
An adult heats the pot gently so the salty water simmers — not a violent boil.
Steam rises, touches the cool lid and condenses into drops that run down and drip into the clean cup.
After several minutes, the adult turns off the heat and lets everything cool before removing the cup.

workedExamples.title: Choosing and Explaining Methods
workedExamples.prompt: Follow the reasoning in each example. In every one, notice how we name the difference between the substances and use it to pick a method.
workedExamples.solution:
Worked Example 1

Question: Halima has a bowl of bariis (rice) with small stones mixed in. How should she separate them, and what property is she using?

Step 1 — Find the difference. The stones and the rice grains are different sizes and colours, and both are solids that are easy to see.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Because the difference is in size and appearance, she can separate them by hand — hand-sorting or sieving the smaller grains from the larger stones.

workedExamples.prompt: Question: Halima has a bowl of bariis (rice) with small stones mixed in. How should she separate them, and what property is she using?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Find the difference. The stones and the rice grains are different sizes and colours, and both are solids that are easy to see.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Because the difference is in size and appearance, she can separate them by hand — hand-sorting or sieving the smaller grains from the larger stones.

Answer: She hand-sorts or sieves them, using the difference in size between the stones and the rice. No dissolving is involved, so no filter or heat is needed.

Worked Example 2

workedExamples.prompt: Question: Farah has salty water and wants to collect the salt. Which method should he use, and what happens to the water?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Find the difference. The salt is dissolved (soluble), so it cannot be filtered. But salt does not evaporate at the temperatures water does.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Since he wants the solid and not the water, he uses evaporation: gently warm the salty water so the water turns to vapour and escapes.

Answer: He uses evaporation. The water escapes into the air as water vapour, and the salt is left behind — exactly as sea-salt farmers do with sunshine.

Worked Example 3

workedExamples.prompt: Question: Khadija has salty water but this time wants the pure water to drink, not the salt. Which method, and why is it different from Example 2?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Find the difference. Water boils and turns to steam at 100 degrees Celsius, but the salt stays behind because it does not turn to gas at that temperature.

Step 2 — Choose the method. Because she wants to keep the water, she must catch the escaping steam and cool it back into a liquid — this is distillation.

Answer: She uses distillation. She boils the salty water, and the steam condenses on a cool lid into pure water, leaving the salt behind. Unlike evaporation, distillation saves the water instead of losing it.

Reading Comprehension — Clean Water in the Dry Season

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: A substance made of only one type of particle is called: (a) a mixture (b) a solution (c) a pure substance (d) a solvent
workedExamples.solution: (c) a pure substance — it is made of only one type of particle.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: In salty water, the salt is the: (a) solvent (b) solute (c) solution (d) filtrate
workedExamples.solution: (b) solute — the salt is the substance that dissolves.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: In salty water, the water is the: (a) solvent (b) solute (c) residue (d) crystal
workedExamples.solution: (a) solvent — the water is the liquid that does the dissolving.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: A substance that does NOT dissolve is described as: (a) soluble (b) saturated (c) insoluble (d) pure

activities.title: Cleaning Muddy Water by Filtration
activities.materials: A cup of clean water with a spoonful of soil, sand or mud stirred in.; A clean cotton cloth or an old (clean) T-shirt, folded several times — or a paper coffee/tea filter.; Two clear cups or jars.; A rubber band or string to hold the cloth over a cup (optional).
steps: Stir the soil into the water so you have a good muddy mixture. Look at it and note its colour.
Fold the cloth several times to make a thick filter, and lay it over the mouth of an empty clean cup.
Slowly pour the muddy water through the cloth into the cup. Do not let it overflow.
Look at the water that has passed through (the filtrate) and at the cloth (the residue).
If the water is still cloudy, pour it through a fresh part of the cloth a second time.

activities.title: Getting Salt Back from Salt Water (Evaporation)
activities.materials: A few spoonfuls of table salt.; Warm water.; A dark-coloured plate or a shallow dish (dark makes the white salt easier to see).; A sunny windowsill or a warm, safe place.; A spoon for stirring.
steps: Dissolve two or three spoonfuls of salt in a small cup of warm water. Stir until the water looks clear and you cannot see the salt any more.
Talk about it: the salt is the solute, the water is the solvent, and the clear salty water is the solution.
Pour a thin layer of the salt solution onto the dark plate.
Put the plate in a warm, sunny place where it will not be disturbed.
Check it once or twice a day for two to four days as the water slowly disappears.

activities.title: Hidden Colours: Paper Chromatography
activities.materials: A strip of white paper towel or a coffee/tea filter, cut about 3 cm wide and 12 cm long.; Water-based felt-tip pens or markers — a black one works best, plus any dark colours. (Avoid permanent markers, which do not dissolve in water.); A clear cup with a little water in the bottom (about 1 cm deep).; A pencil and some tape to hang the strip.
steps: Draw a thick dot of ink about 2 cm up from the bottom end of the paper strip. Press hard so the colour is strong.
Pour about 1 cm of water into the cup.
Hang the strip so its bottom edge just dips into the water, but the ink dot stays ABOVE the water line. Tape the top to a pencil laid across the cup.
Watch as the water slowly climbs up the paper and reaches the ink dot.
Leave it for 10 to 20 minutes as the water carries the colours up the paper.

activities.title: The Dissolving and Saturation Test
activities.materials: Table salt or sugar.; Three clear cups: one with cold water, one with warm water, one with hot water (an adult handles the hot water).; A spoon for stirring and a teaspoon for measuring.; Optional: a small lump of rock salt or sugar cube to compare with the fine grains.
steps: Part A — Temperature: Put one level spoonful of salt into each of the cold, warm and hot cups at the same time. Do NOT stir. Watch and time how long each takes to disappear.
Part B — Stirring: Add another spoonful to the cold cup and this time stir it. Does it dissolve faster than the one you did not stir?
Part C — Grain size (optional): Drop a sugar cube and the same amount of loose sugar into two cups of the same temperature. Which dissolves first?
Part D — Saturation: Take the hot-water cup. Keep adding salt one spoonful at a time, stirring after each, and counting the spoonfuls, until no more will dissolve and it collects at the bottom.
Record all your results in the table.

activities.title: Catching Pure Water (Simple Distillation)
activities.materials: A cooking pot with a lid (a domed lid works best).; Salty water (a spoonful of salt stirred into water).; A small clean heatproof cup or bowl that fits inside the pot.; An adult to manage the stove and the hot pot — this experiment uses heat.
steps: An adult pours the salty water into the pot to a shallow depth, and stands the empty clean cup in the middle so its rim is above the water.
Put the lid on the pot UPSIDE DOWN (so the dome points inwards, guiding drips towards the cup).
An adult heats the pot gently so the salty water simmers — not a violent boil.
Steam rises, touches the cool lid and condenses into drops that run down and drip into the clean cup.
After several minutes, the adult turns off the heat and lets everything cool before removing the cup.

activities.title: Observe: A worked real-life example - cleaning muddy, salty water
activities.materials: A cup of clean water with a spoonful of soil, sand or mud stirred in.; A clean cotton cloth or an old (clean) T-shirt, folded several times — or a paper coffee/tea filter.; Two clear cups or jars.; A rubber band or string to hold the cloth over a cup (optional).
steps: Look for an example of a worked real-life example — cleaning muddy, salty water around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Pure substance and Mixture.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Filtration Does Not Make Water Safe
rules.text: Filtration removes only solid bits you can catch — it does NOT remove dissolved salt or kill germs. Filtered water still needs to be BOILED before it is safe to drink. Evaporation keeps the solid; distillation keeps the pure liquid.

rules.title: Mixtures and How to Separate Them
rules.text: A mixture is not chemically joined, so its parts keep their properties and can be separated again. Solute + solvent = solution. Filtration keeps insoluble solids; evaporation keeps dissolved solids; distillation keeps pure liquid; chromatography separates dyes. Always make water safe: filter to clear it, then BOIL it to kill germs before drinking.

terms: Pure substance
Made of only one type of particle; has a fixed melting and boiling point.
Mixture
Two or more substances mixed but not chemically joined; parts can be separated.
Solution
A mixture where a solute is fully dissolved in a solvent; looks clear.
Solvent
The liquid that does the dissolving (usually water).
Solute
The substance that dissolves into the solvent.
Dissolve
When a solute breaks up and spreads evenly through a solvent.
Soluble
Able to dissolve in a solvent.
Insoluble
Not able to dissolve; stays as solid bits.
Solubility
How much solute dissolves in a solvent at a given temperature.
Saturated solution
A solution holding as much dissolved solute as it possibly can.
Filtration
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using a filter.
Residue
The solid left behind on the filter.

realProblems.answer: 1. First filter the muddy water through a clean cloth to remove the mud and sand (the residue), giving clearer water. Then boil that filtered water for several minutes to kill the germs. Only after boiling is it safe to drink. (If the water were also salty, he would need to distil it.)

realProblems.prompt: A mixture contains sand, salt and water all together. Describe, in the correct order, how you would separate all three, and explain why the order matters.
realProblems.answer: 1. First filter the mixture: the insoluble sand is caught as residue, and salty water passes through as filtrate. Then evaporate (or distil) the salty water: if you evaporate it, the water leaves and the salt is left behind; if you distil it, you also collect the pure water. The order matters because you must remove the insoluble sand first — trying to separate the salt while the sand is still mixed in would leave sand in your product.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between a pure substance and a mixture.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1. A pure substance is made of only one type of particle, with nothing mixed in (like pure water). A mixture is two or more substances mixed together but not chemically joined (like sea water), and its parts can be separated again.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Define the words solute, solvent and solution, using sweet shaah as your example.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 2. In sweet shaah, the solute is the sugar (the thing that dissolves), the solvent is the water (the liquid that dissolves it), and the solution is the sweet tea you get when the sugar has dissolved evenly.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between soluble and insoluble? Give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3. Soluble means able to dissolve (for example, salt or sugar in water). Insoluble means unable to dissolve (for example, sand or oil in water).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name three things you can do to make a solid dissolve faster.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 4. Any three of: heat the solvent (warm water); stir the mixture; crush the solid into smaller pieces or powder.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is a saturated solution? What happens if you cool a hot saturated solution?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5. A saturated solution is one holding as much dissolved solute as it possibly can. If you cool a hot saturated solution, it can no longer hold all the solute, so the extra solute comes out as solid crystals.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe how filtration works, using the words residue and filtrate.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 6. In filtration you pour the mixture through filter paper or cloth. The insoluble solid is too big to pass through and is trapped as the residue; the liquid passes through as the filtrate.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit you will be able to:
I can explain the difference between a pure substance and a mixture, and give everyday examples of each.
I can define and use the words solution, solvent, solute and dissolve correctly.
I can describe what solubility means and list the factors that make a solid dissolve faster.
I can explain what a saturated solution is and how it forms.
I can choose and describe the correct separation method — filtration, evaporation, crystallisation, distillation or chromatography — for a given mixture.
I can explain how each separation method works using the different properties of the substances involved.
I can apply these methods to real problems such as getting clean water from muddy or salty water.
